title: CJP's 'Chalo Sansad' March Draws Thousands as Protest Movement Goes Global
excerpt: The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party staged its boldest action yet with a march toward Parliament on the first day of the monsoon session, while Indian students abroad amplified calls for the education minister's resignation.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Thousands joined the Cockroach Janta Party's 'Chalo Sansad' march on July 20.
  • CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke is on an indefinite hunger strike.
  • The movement has over 22 million Instagram followers, gaining international support.
  • Delhi Police enforced prohibitory orders to prevent the march from reaching Parliament.
  • The CJP demands the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over examination irregularities.

Major Demands: Minister's Resignation
CJP Movement Overview

What began as a satirical social media campaign two months ago escalated into one of India's most significant youth-led protests on Sunday, when thousands of supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party attempted to march from Jantar Mantar to Parliament on the first day of the monsoon session.

Delhi Police had imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, banning gatherings of five or more persons near Parliament, and deployed additional personnel at key locations including Parliament Street, Central Vista, Connaught Place and Shankar Chowk. Barricades were erected along the planned march route.

From Online Satire to Street Mobilisation

The CJP emerged in May after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant called young critics of the government "cockroaches" and "parasites" during a hearing. Abhijeet Dipke, a political communications strategist and Boston University student, reappropriated the slur to launch a parody political party that rapidly amassed over 22 million Instagram followers.

The movement's central demand — the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in NEET, CBSE, CUET and SSC examinations — has drawn broad support from students, parents and civil society figures. Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk joined the protests early on, describing himself as an "honorary cockroach."

"If the government is stubborn, we are more stubborn."

— Abhijeet Dipke, Founder, Cockroach Janta Party

Hunger Strikes and Hospitalisation

The situation at Jantar Mantar grew more urgent in the days before the march. Wangchuk's health deteriorated during his hunger strike, and he was moved to Safdarjung Hospital following a Delhi High Court order. Dipke subsequently began his own indefinite hunger strike, with the CJP saying the decision reflected the government's refusal to engage with their demands.

Aazad Samaj Party chief and MP Chandrashekhar Azad backed the protest, pledging to raise the students' concerns in Parliament. The CJP said it remained willing to enter dialogue, but only on the condition that Pradhan step down first.

Diaspora Connections Run Deep

The movement's international dimension has been evident from the outset. Dipke himself flew from the United States to lead the first protest at Jantar Mantar on June 6, with the BJP later taking a veiled dig at "some people sitting abroad" who think they can direct India's youth.

The confrontation extended to London in early June, when Chief Justice Surya Kant delivered a lecture on artificial intelligence at Birkbeck College, University of London. Attendees attempted to question him about dissent and democratic freedoms in India, leading to a tense exchange when organisers restricted the discussion to the stated topic. CJP spokesperson Saurav Das shared footage of the incident, which circulated widely on social media.

Indian students at universities across the UK and the United States have organised solidarity campaigns online, sharing protest imagery and amplifying the CJP's demands through diaspora networks. The movement's reach reflects a broader trend of South Asian youth movements born on social media translating into real-world political action, echoing earlier uprisings in Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

Government Response Hardens

Education Minister Pradhan has not responded to the resignation demands. He has instead accused the CJP of being a "B-team of terrorists" and described the movement as comprising "disruptive elements intent on breaking up the nation."

The government's response prompted Dipke to challenge the characterisation: "Are we asking for votes? We are asking for justice. We are taxpayers, our parents are taxpayers, and you call us terrorists. Are you not ashamed?"

The CJP has said it will continue its sit-in at Jantar Mantar until its demands are met. With the monsoon session under way and the opposition likely to raise examination-related issues in Parliament, the pressure on the education ministry shows no sign of easing.
